extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers conducting structural equation modeling (SEM) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in the social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for identifying, screening, estimating, modifying, and validating structural equation models and measurement models (CFAs), including sample-size rules, missing-data handling, assumption checks, fit-index interpretation, and acceptable model-modification practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model identification — unique solution for every parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Every unknown parameter must have a unique solution in order to be identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only fool-proof method is to depict identification algebraically (often difficult for complex models). Follow identification rules such as the three-indicator rule, but recognize these are sufficient not necessary conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-indicator rule (local identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are three or more indicators per latent variable, identification may be met (the 'three-indicator rule').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a commonly-cited sufficient condition for CFA identification. A model may still be identified with fewer than three indicators, but small samples increase risk of estimation problems when constructs have only two indicators (see Kline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-indicator rule (sufficient condition reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bollen's 'two-indicator rule' is one of the sufficient conditions for identification in CFA models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced as an example of alternative sufficient conditions; treat as a specialist exception rather than a general recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive-model rule for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: If the model is recursive (no feedback loops between constructs and no correlated error/disturbance terms), then it is identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check model structure for feedback loops and correlated disturbances; if absent, identification follows under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample-size rule of thumb: 10 cases per parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: A general rule of thumb for SEM and CFA is to have approximately 10 cases per parameter to estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a model-development approach that splits the data into exploratory and confirmatory subsamples, double the required sample (e.g., 28 parameters → 280 cases; for split approach require 560 = 280 x 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case retention criterion for missing data (study-specific example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain only cases with complete values for a prespecified proportion of measured variables (example: retained cases with complete values for 9 of 13 measured variables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study, cases missing more than 30% (five or more) variables were deleted. Apply an explicit threshold appropriate to your study and report it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing-data handling: Expectation-Maximization (EM) imputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Impute missing values using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm when using ML estimation that assumes no missing data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EM was chosen because comparative studies (e.g., Gold & Bentler 2000) favored EM methods across proportions of missing data, distributional characteristics, and sample sizes. Report justification and method used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-screening checklist before SEM
rubrics_metrics.description: Screen data by examining descriptive statistics, checking for linearity, identifying outliers/extreme cases, and assessing multivariate normality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine means, SDs, min/max, bivariate scatterplots for linearity, univariate boxplots for outliers, and multivariate normality diagnostics (e.g., Mardia's coefficient). Keep suspicious cases in mind for possible omission and document decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlier detection with Mahalanobis distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify multivariate outliers via Mahalanobis distance and remove cases that exceed the critical value and show jumps from neighboring cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Mahalanobis values alongside univariate diagnostics (boxplots) and inspect for 'jumps' in values; removal decisions should be justified and reported (example: five cases removed for large Mahalanobis and jumps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivariate normality assessment using Mardia’s coefficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess multivariate kurtosis with Mardia’s coefficient to evaluate departures from multivariate normality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mardia’s coefficient can be interpreted as a z-score (traditional outlier cutoff ≈ 3). Large sample sizes can inflate the magnitude; interpret in context and consider follow-up validation (e.g., bootstrapping) if slightly elevated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate ML results when non-normality suspected: Bollen–Stine bootstrap
rubrics_metrics.description: When multivariate normality is questionable, validate ML estimation results using Bollen–Stine bootstrapping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If bootstrapped output verifies ML estimates, ML outputs may be reported; otherwise report bootstrap-corrected results. Document p-close and bootstrap diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumptions include independence of observations, proper model specification, multivariate normality of the endogenous variables, and independence of the exogenous variables and disturbances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify sampling/procedures support independence (e.g., only one survey response per participant). Explicitly assess and report each assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step modeling approach (measurement then structural)
rubrics_metrics.description: First validate the measurement model (CFA) with all plausible associations among latent constructs, then evaluate the full structural model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement model assessment includes examining factor loadings, covariance coefficients, and model fit before interpreting structural paths; if the CFA fits poorly, respecification is necessary before trusting structural results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement-model assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess measurement model by (a) examining factor loadings to ensure indicator paths are significant, (b) reviewing covariance coefficients, and (c) assessing model fit with goodness-of-fit indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If loadings are low or nonsignificant, consider omitting or relocating indicators, guided by theory and prior research. Reassess construct reliabilities after any changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modification indices (MIs) guided by theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Use modification indices to suggest model changes but implement only those that are 'facially valid' and consistent with theory and prior research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples implemented only when justified: correlating error terms due to common response scales, conceptual overlap (e.g., both are information subsidies), or opposite question wording producing negative correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for correlating measurement errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlate measurement errors only when there is a substantive rationale (e.g., same response scale causing method effects, conceptually similar indicators such as information subsidies, or opposite question wording).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear substantive justification for each correlated error (study gave three examples: shared response scale, both indicators are information subsidies, and opposite wording producing negative correlation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-fit indices to report and interpret
rubrics_metrics.description: Report chi-squared statistic, SRMR, RMSEA with p-close and 90% CI, TLI (Tucker–Lewis Index), and CFI (Comparative Fit Index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret chi-squared as a 'badness-of-fit' index (nonsignificant desired, though sensitive to sample size). Present both absolute and relative fit indices and justify chosen cutoff criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit-index cutoff heuristics (traditional and Hu & Bentler)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional rules of thumb: nonsignificant χ2 (rare with large samples), SRMR < .10, CFI and TLI ≥ .90; RMSEA ≤ .05 close fit, .05–.08 reasonable, ≥ .10 poor. Kline recommends reporting 90% CI for RMSEA with lower ≤ .05 and upper ≤ .10; p-close should be nonsignificant (> .05). Hu & Bentler suggested stricter cutoffs: SRMR ≈ .08, CFI/TLI ≈ .95, RMSEA ≈ .06 (p-close ≥ .05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both traditional and more stringent recommendations, but be cautious: Hu & Bentler's cutoffs have limitations and may be overgeneralized; discuss appropriateness for sample size/model complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct/parameter assessments using correlations and regressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correlation and multiple regression analyses (including partial correlations) to address hypotheses about relationships between measures and to assess predictor strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example uses: zero-order correlations for primary hypotheses; partial correlations to control for market size; multiple regressions to evaluate relative predictive strength of extramedia and organizational measures. Ensure assumptions for multiple regression (multivariate normality, linearity, normally distributed residuals) are checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting latent constructs to observed variables for regression
rubrics_metrics.description: To use a latent construct in regression, compute an observed score by multiplying factor score coefficients by each indicator value and summing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example formula: (coefficient1 × agenda_building) + (coefficient2 × frame_building) + (coefficient3 × agenda_cutting) = observed content influence/outcome variable. Document method and coefficients used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report scale reliabilities after model modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: After changing indicator inclusion or placement, reassess and report reliability coefficients (e.g., Cronbach’s alpha) for measured variables and their constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if item-level reliabilities didn't change, construct reliabilities may change when indicators are moved or omitted; provide a summary table of alphas to inform readers of measure strength (study reported alphas for all scales).
